briefing_md:
Regime read: recession risk has decisively faded and credit is priced for perfection, but the dominant macro risk has rotated from growth to a back-end-led inflation/rates shock under a new Fed chair.

The ensemble recession gauge sits at the 40th percentile of the last 5y (19.6%, -4.2pp over three months), with the NY Fed probit at 29.6th and the NTFS logit at 23.3rd — all decelerating. The near-term forward spread has flipped firmly positive (74th percentile, +51bps in 3m) and 10y–3m has steepened to the 76th percentile. This is not what an oncoming recession looks like. The trigger for that move is visible in the news flow: a blowout May payrolls print, eurozone CPI at 3.2%, U.S. CPI projected to breach 4%, and ECB/Fed both telegraphing an extended hold. DGS10 at the 87th percentile (4.45%, +30bps in 3m) while DGS2 also bid up is a bear-steepening driven by inflation re-acceleration and a $646bn weekly Treasury supply slug, not growth optimism.

Credit conditions remain unambiguously easy. GZ spread is at the 0th percentile of the 5y (0.83pp — a 5y low), EBP at the 13.6th (-0.39pp), OFR FSI at the 33.8th, HYG +6.5% y/y. The credit impulse has swung to the 89.5th percentile. Yet Pimco is warning the default cycle is resuming, and the tape supports it: Sleep Number Chapter 11 ($415mn debt), GoHealth, GoldenPeaks' 40-debtor SDTX filing, Ritz-Carlton Yacht amend-and-extend with a $275mn equity injection. Bath & Body Works at 7.7% YTW on 2.0x leverage suggests idiosyncratic re-pricing under the index calm.

Consumer credit is mixed-to-stable: card 90+ DQ at the 42nd percentile and ticking down, card NCOs at the 47th, but single-family mortgage DQ has pushed to the 73.7th percentile (1.89%, +11bps) — the one consumer line that is quietly worsening as the 10y stays bid. BNPL bleeding into gas, groceries, and rent is a stress tell that the aggregate prints don't capture.

Structured finance is firmly risk-on. Prime auto senior at 45bps (-8 vs prior), subprime auto senior at 72bps, mezz tightening across stacks. EDGAR shows 160 data-center and 175 royalty filings in 30 days, alongside the $35bn Apollo/Blackstone Anthropic private credit deal — AI infrastructure is the new dominant ABS theme.

Regulatory wildcard: Warsh's first FOMC, a Fed "payment account" proposal, DOJ debanking subpoenas, and a four-country Asian/Gulf cross-border CBDC platform challenging dollar rails.

news_digests_recent.summary:
The dominant story this week is the debut of Kevin Warsh as Federal Reserve chair, with markets on edge ahead of his first press conference and policy meeting. Economists and strategists, including Bloomberg Intelligence's Ira Jersey, admit they have little read on his inclinations — an unusual degree of uncertainty for a Fed transition. Pimco added to the cautious tone, warning that defaults in debt markets are resuming and urging investors to rotate into fixed income as equity valuations look stretched. Meanwhile, the Treasury sold $646 billion in securities in a single week, with net notes and bonds outstanding rising $59 billion, and analysts flagging a potential second wave of inflation pressuring the 10-year yield. Japan's long-bond market saw renewed selling as global funds retreated after the BOJ's slow normalization pace disappointed expectations built over the past year.

On credit, the default cycle Pimco flagged is already visible. Sleep Number Corp. filed Chapter 11 on June 12 with roughly $415 million in debt, joined in recent weeks by GoHealth (a prepackaged deleveraging), SiFi Networks America (a cleanse-and-repurchase fiber deal), and GoldenPeaks Poland Holding — 40 affiliated debtors filed in the Southern District of Texas on May 29. Sovereign credit also moved: Lazard is making a late push to displace Centerview as Venezuela's restructuring adviser, undercutting on fees for what would rank among the largest sovereign debt workouts on record.

Private credit is crowding out traditional fixed income allocation debates. Apollo published multiple pieces this week positioning private IG credit as a portfolio anchor, framing private market secondaries — pegged at a $225 billion market — as a core allocation offering instant diversification and accelerated cash flows relative to primary PE, which faces a record exit backlog. The convergence of public and private credit markets is a running theme, with extended holding periods pushing more capital toward secondaries.

In fintech and regulatory, DOJ debanking subpoenas are emerging as part of a broader supervisory puzzle. Democratic senators are urging the Fed and OCC to block the Grasshopper bank acquisition, Trump nominated a new CFPB director, and Colorado's governor vetoed a state interchange law. China separately advanced a cross-border digital payments platform backed by the central banks of Hong Kong, Thailand, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia — a direct challenge to dollar payment rails.

The dominant macro signal this week is a looming U.S. inflation breakout: consumer prices are forecast to breach 4% for the first time since 2023, putting the Federal Reserve squarely back under pressure. New York Fed survey data reinforce the strain, with household financial worries hitting their highest level since July 2022. Treasury yields edged higher as markets digested the Middle East conflict — the Iran war is already lifting oil demand and pushing the Bank of France to revise its 2026 inflation forecast upward. The WSJ Dollar Index slipped 0.10% to 96.50, reflecting broader uncertainty around U.S. rate trajectory as Kevin Warsh prepares for his first rate-setting meeting as Fed chair.

The rate-hike impulse is spreading beyond the U.S. Markets are now pricing an ECB rate increase — its first in nearly three years — though at least one prominent economist has labeled it a policy mistake. Indonesia delivered a shock off-cycle rate hike to arrest a currency and equity selloff triggered by political uncertainty under President Prabowo, a move aimed squarely at halting foreign outflows.

In structured finance and private credit, deal flow remains robust. Unlock Technologies and D2 Asset Management closed a $358.5 million home equity agreement securitization. Manulife's Comvest Credit Partners priced a $428 million CLO. Canyon Partners launched Canyon ABF Partners, an expanded asset-backed finance platform, hiring the former Atlas CEO to lead the venture. Most significantly, Apollo and Blackstone jointly raised $35 billion in chip financing for Anthropic in what ranks among the largest private credit transactions on record.

On the consumer credit front, "rent now, pay later" products are gaining traction as housing affordability deteriorates, extending the BNPL model into the rental market. BDC redemption activity has resumed, with Crescent Capital, Eurazeo, HSBC AM, and PGIM among those raising fresh capital — a signal that institutional appetite for private lending vehicles remains intact despite the macro headwinds.

The dominant market-moving event is the May U.S. non-farm payrolls print, which came in roughly twice consensus expectations with the unemployment rate holding steady. The blowout report has effectively closed the door on Federal Reserve rate cuts and reopened the debate about hikes. Treasury yields and the dollar both rose on the data, gold slumped, and stocks reversed a historic weekly winning streak as equity and bond markets repriced simultaneously. BlackRock's Jeffrey Rosenberg noted markets are now "on the precipice of pricing in a full rate hike" for 2025, though policymakers are in no hurry to move. Wolfe Research's Stephanie Roth pushed back modestly, arguing inflation is not accelerating in a material way, leaving the Fed in a data-dependent holding pattern focused on prices rather than employment.

The strong U.S. print reverberated globally. Emerging-market currencies sank across the board as the case for EM-supportive Fed easing evaporated. India faces compounding pressures — the RBI held rates despite rupee weakness from foreign outflows tied to the Iran war, and the government exempted foreign investors from bond taxes to shore up inflows, a measure analysts cautioned is a band-aid given deeper structural headwinds. Fitch cut its global growth outlook to reflect the Middle East conflict's drag, and the eurozone reported a first-quarter GDP contraction with the Iran war darkening the forward outlook further.

Elsewhere in developed markets, Bank of Japan rate-rise bets firmed after April cash earnings posted their strongest growth since late 2024, while the ECB is seen as capable of hiking even into a gradually weakening eurozone economy as inflation concerns dominate. Japan's prime minister reiterated yen defense through economic strengthening rather than direct intervention.

On credit and structured themes, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac shares whipsawed after President Trump floated a combined valuation of roughly $1 trillion for the GSEs, with an intraday rally largely fading on investor skepticism. In credit markets, tech issuers are monetizing AI-driven equity volatility through elevated convertible bond supply, and Colombian bond investors are positioning around a right-wing presidential candidate pledging sharp fiscal consolidation.

Eurozone inflation jumping to 3.2% in May — a near three-year high driven by a 10.9% annual surge in energy costs tied to the Iran conflict — is the dominant macro signal of the moment. Core inflation is also firming, and the ECB appears locked into a rate hike at its June meeting. Simultaneously, new Iran-related military clashes are sending oil prices and bond yields higher in tandem, compressing the window for any central bank patience on either side of the Atlantic.

On the Fed side, Cleveland's Hammack flagged that the Fed may need to respond if inflation proves persistent, reinforcing a higher-for-longer posture. April U.S. job openings surged to 7.6 million — up 731,000 month-on-month and the highest in nearly two years — removing any near-term justification for easing. Treasury yields and the dollar turned modestly higher in response. Gold has meanwhile displaced U.S. Treasuries as the world's top reserve asset, per the ECB, with bullion now comprising 27% of global reserves as central banks diversify away from dollar holdings.

In credit, the Optimum-Apollo-Ares dispute over asset transfers has escalated sharply, threatening to become a defining liability-management test case in distressed debt. Venezuela has retained Hogan Lovells for what is shaping up as one of the largest sovereign restructurings in decades. Castlelake, the $37 billion manager, is reportedly eyeing a bid for easyJet, illustrating private credit's continued push into aviation and operating assets. U.S. convertible bond issuance is tracking toward a record year as issuers exploit AI-driven equity momentum to place zero-coupon paper.

On the consumer and fintech front, Americans are increasingly using buy-now-pay-later for gas and groceries — a stress signal given pump prices are running more than a dollar per gallon above year-ago levels. Wise faces a money-laundering investigation at a particularly fraught moment following its transatlantic listing. In structured finance, CLO ETFs are being positioned as a cash-management alternative, reflecting sustained institutional appetite for floating-rate, highly rated paper.

The dominant story this week is the Fed's institutional integrity under fire. Former Chair Jerome Powell, speaking at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, warned that the central bank is undergoing a "stress test" as political pressure — specifically Trump's attempts to remove central bankers — undermines rule of law. Powell's remarks, described as a pointed warning wrapped in abstraction, came alongside signals from both the Fed and Bank of England that neither institution sees reason to shift policy imminently, favoring an active hold. Bond traders, meanwhile, are positioned for a Fed rate hike by next year, with a key jobs report this week set to test that conviction.

In leveraged credit, QXO Building Products launched a $3 billion loan sale via Wells Fargo to finance its acquisition of TopBuild Corp., one of the larger M&A debt packages in recent weeks. The deal lands in a market where sector labels are proving unreliable guides — Credit Weekly flags that safe-looking names are getting hit while apparently distressed ones survive, a reminder that binary credit framing is breaking down. The Ritz-Carlton Yacht restructuring illustrates the point: lenders agreed to ease terms and push back payment dates after owners injected $275 million fresh equity to keep the luxury cruise line solvent.

In structured finance, GreatAmerica closed a $747 million equipment finance securitization, continuing steady issuance in the ABS complex. On the rates side, Candriam is favoring 10-year German Bunds while growing more cautious on select other eurozone sovereigns.

Fintech faces its own pressure: Wise shares slumped after the London-based payments company disclosed it is responding to a money laundering investigation from Belgian authorities. In emerging markets, Chilean investors are rotating back into short-term peso bonds as Iran-war inflation fears recede, and Jefferies floated the idea of a US dollar swap line for Turkey ahead of elections to stabilize hard-currency reserves.

Bond traders are bracing for this week's US jobs report as the definitive test of whether the economy can sustain Federal Reserve rate hikes by next year — the single most consequential data point in a week crowded with central bank signals. The Fed and Bank of England both telegraphed an extended hold at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, citing AI productivity dynamics and energy price behavior as justification for patience. Fed Governor Christopher Waller added a structural dimension, arguing that stablecoin proliferation could amplify the reach of US monetary policy globally — a notable acknowledgment that dollar-denominated digital instruments are becoming a transmission channel. Kevin Warsh is separately pushing the Fed to reconceptualize its inflation framework, while ECB Governing Council member Alvaro Santos Pereira broke from the hold consensus, calling for the ECB to act sooner given persistent consumer-price pressure in Europe.

In credit, the stress at Ritz-Carlton Yacht crystallized the divide between distressed leisure travel and buoyant broader markets: owners injected $275 million while lenders agreed to delay payments and loosen covenants, a classic amend-and-extend under duress. Bath & Body Works bonds at 7.7% YTW are drawing scrutiny despite 2.0x leverage, $600 million of free cash flow, and no maturities until 2028 — the spread implying the market is pricing something beyond the headline metrics. Wall Street bulls are otherwise shrugging off bubble concerns in equities, concentrating bets on AI-linked names.

In emerging markets, record inflows to hard-currency EM debt have become so intense that two specialist hedge funds have begun turning away capital — a crowding signal worth monitoring as a contrarian indicator. China's manufacturing activity remained flat in May, weighed by elevated energy costs, adding a soft patch to the global demand picture. On the fintech and regulatory front, ICBA formally asked the OCC to rescind Coinbase's conditional bank charter approval, escalating traditional banking's pushback against crypto institutional entry.
